possible: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (if AFB smear positive but culture/PCR does not confirm M. tuberculosis)
pathogens.why: The clinical syndrome of prolonged cough with constitutional symptoms (weight loss, evening fever, night sweats) in an endemic country is classically tuberculous, but microbiological confirmation remains essential since the clinical picture alone is not specific enough to justify treatment, which carries real toxicity and public health implications (resistance, contact tracing).

investigations.test: Sputum smear for AFB (at least 2 samples)
investigations.why: Rapid, widely available test; positive smear supports diagnosis and indicates infectiousness for public health purposes.

investigations.test: CBNAAT / Xpert MTB-RIF (or equivalent rapid molecular test)
investigations.why: Provides faster diagnosis than culture and simultaneously detects rifampicin resistance, directly informing regimen choice — should be prioritized where available.
Gold standard for diagnosis and allows full drug-susceptibility testing if initial molecular testing suggests resistance or treatment failure occurs.
Supports diagnosis (upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation) and provides a baseline for treatment response monitoring.
TB-HIV co-infection changes management (ART timing, drug interactions) and is a standard part of TB workup per national guidelines.
